title: Pseudorandom Functions: Direct Access to Huge Pseudorandom Objects

reading.text: Self-contained lesson. Optional background: Goldreich's Primer, Ch. 2.7.2 (pseudorandom functions).

body:
## From generators to functions: a change of access model

A pseudorandom generator $G: \{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^{\ell(k)}$ hides a long string behind a short seed: any efficient observer must confuse $G(U_k)$ with $U_{\ell(k)}$. But a PRG offers **sequential** access only. A consumer who needs "the bits at positions of its choosing" must run the generator and work through its output; the object behind the seed has no identity beyond that stream. Now imagine two parties who share a seed and will later need to agree — **without any further communication** — on random-looking values attached to data items that neither of them knows in advance. If the items range over the huge set $\{0,1\}^k$, pre-generating a value for every possible item would require materializing an exponentially long string. What they need is a *function*, not a string.

Pseudorandom functions are the answer. As the Primer puts it in §2.7.2, whereas generators provide a way to efficiently generate long pseudorandom *sequences* from short random seeds, pseudorandom functions are even more powerful: they provide **efficient direct access to the bits of a huge pseudorandom sequence, which is not feasible to scan bit-by-bit**. A seed $s \in \{0,1\}^k$ names one function

$$f_s: \{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^k$$

out of the $2^k$ candidates in the family — while a truly random function of this type is one among $2^{k \cdot 2^k}$ functions — and $f_s(x)$ can be computed in polynomial time at any point $x$ we choose, whenever we choose it. Random access to an exponential table, through a polynomial-time interface.

The shift of perspective is the theme of this module: randomness stops being a static string and becomes a dynamic object — a black box that answers fresh queries with values that look random, yet stay perfectly consistent and reproducible from the seed.

## Definition 2.17: pseudorandom functions

The formal object is a **function ensemble**: a collection of functions indexed by seeds, with one requirement about *computing* them and one about *hiding* them.

@def:prf

Read the definition against the PRG definition you already know (Definition 2.1):

- **Where the string was, a function now stands.** The candidate object is a random member of the family $\{f_s\}_{s}$, i.e., a distribution over "tables" of $k \cdot 2^k$ bits — except that no one ever materializes the table. Only its values at requested points ever appear, and only polynomially many of them.
- **Efficient evaluation is what makes the object usable.** Condition (1) asks for a single deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the map $(s, x) \mapsto f_s(x)$. Note what it does *not* require: nothing about the description size of $f_s$ (the description is never revealed), no short circuit or formula for $f_s$, and no way to act on $f_s$ other than querying it.
- **The distinguisher is upgraded from a machine that reads a string into a machine that interrogates an oracle.** This is forced by the nature of the object and mirrors how PRFs are used: in every application, parties interact with $f_s$ solely by choosing arguments and reading off the answers.

## The oracle model: testing a function you can only query

@def:oracle-model

Why is this the right model? Because it is the only feasible one, and the only faithful one:

- **A description is too large to give and too large to hide.** An explicit description of a function $\{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^k$ has $k \cdot 2^k$ bits. Worse, in the random-function experiment there is no seed at all — handing $s$ to $M$ in the pseudorandom experiment would destroy the symmetry between the two experiments, and handing a truth table would make both experiments exponentially slow.
- **Oracle access captures how the object is actually used.** Parties share $s$; everything anyone ever learns about $f_s$ is learned through evaluations. The definition certifies precisely the property that applications consume: no efficient party restricted to queries can tell $f_s$ (for random $s$) apart from a truly random function.
- **The machine is probabilistic and receives the length parameter.** $M$ runs in time polynomial in $k$, may toss coins, and may ask polynomially many queries of length $k$; the input $1^k$ (the seed length written in unary) is what makes "polynomial in $k$" well defined.

### Adaptive queries, and why one output bit is enough

A *non-adaptive* machine fixes its whole list of queries in advance and reads the answers afterwards; an *adaptive* machine may let each query depend on the answers seen so far. Adaptivity is genuinely more powerful: a machine that queries $x$, receives $y$, and then queries $y$ can detect relations such as $f_s(f_s(x))$ that no fixed list could aim at. Since every non-adaptive machine is a special case of an adaptive one, quantifying over adaptive machines yields the stronger — and safe — requirement, and Definition 2.17 does exactly that.

Why may the output be a single bit? Because a distinguisher is, by definition, a yes/no decision. Any test that returns a richer verdict — a string, a real-valued statistic, a guess at the seed — can be wrapped: run it internally and output 1 exactly when the verdict falls in the accepting set. Multi-bit outputs and multiple statistical tests therefore add no power, and the one-bit convention keeps the formulation clean. (The "probabilistic" in "probabilistic polynomial-time oracle machine" matters: the probabilities in condition (2) are taken over the choice of oracle *and* over $M$'s internal coin tosses.)

## Variants and immediate adjustments

Definition 2.17 fixes domain = range = seed length, and an argument length equal to $|s|$. Useful variants, noted right after Theorem 2.18 in the Primer, include:

- **Boolean pseudorandom functions over all strings**: $f_s: \{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}$, where the argument may have any length.
- **General domain and range**: $f_s: \{0,1\}^{d(|s|)} \to \{0,1\}^{r(|s|)}$ for arbitrary polynomially bounded functions $d, r: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$.
- **Transformations between variants** are known (cf. [17, Sec. 3.6.4] and [18, Apdx. C.2]), so the choice of variant is mostly a matter of convenience.
- **Stronger distinguishers.** As §2.7.1 stresses for generators, the definition can be strengthened by quantifying the distinguisher's resources (and gaps) explicitly as functions of the seed length, or by moving to non-uniform distinguishers. Non-uniform versions of pseudorandom functions — strengthening Definition 2.15's analogue — are of independent interest and resurface in Module 6.

In every variant the security condition is the same oracle-indistinguishability game, with only the domain and range adjusted.

## PRFs already give PRGs

The definition is only useful if such ensembles exist; Theorem 2.18 — the GGM construction of pseudorandom functions from any pseudorandom generator — is the subject of the next lesson. One direction is nearly free, and proving it carefully is the best way to internalize the definition.

@thm:prf-prg

The proof is a direct reduction of exactly the shape used throughout the course:

- Take any PPT distinguisher $D$ attacking $G$.
- Build an oracle machine $M$ attacking the PRF: $M$ queries its oracle at the fixed points $x_1, \ldots, x_{m(k)}$, concatenates the answers, and hands the resulting string to $D$.
- When $M$'s oracle is $f_{U_k}$, the string $D$ sees is distributed as $G(U_k)$; when it is $F_k$, the answers at the *pairwise distinct* points are independent and uniform, so the string is distributed exactly as $U_{m(k) \cdot k}$. Hence $M$'s distinguishing gap equals $D$'s, and Definition 2.17 forces it to be negligible.
- **Why fixed, non-adaptive queries are legitimate:** the pseudorandomness condition quantifies over *every* PPT oracle machine — in particular over machines whose query list is hard-wired in advance. We are not required to exploit adaptivity for the definition to apply; that adaptivity is *permitted* only makes the definition harder to satisfy and the reduction sound.
- **Where distinctness is used:** a truly random $F_k$ returns the same value when queried twice at the same point, and independent uniform values at distinct points. The "ideal" string is uniform *because* the $x_i$'s are pairwise distinct; had two coincide, the ideal string would contain a duplicated block and would be easy to distinguish.

## Sharing a seed is agreeing on $2^k$ random values "on the fly"

The key feature of pseudorandom functions, stressed in the Primer, is that the function is *fully determined by its seed* and can therefore be **generated and shared by merely generating and sharing the seed**. Two parties who share $s$ can, at any later moment, associate to any value $v \in \{0,1\}^k$ the random-looking value $r_v = f_s(v)$:

- **Agreement with zero communication.** Because $f_s$ is a genuine function, every party computes the *same* $r_v$ from the same $v$. No synchronization, no a priori list of items, no further messages: the association is fixed once and for all by the seed. One party randomly selects $s$ and communicates it once, over a secure channel.
- **Fresh-looking randomness, on-line.** To any efficient adversary who does not know $s$ — including one who picks items $v$ adaptively, after seeing earlier values — the answers at new, unqueried points are indistinguishable from the answers of a truly random function. This is exactly the oracle-indistinguishability condition, with the adversary playing the role of $M$.
- **One seed hides $2^k$ values.** The parties are committed to random-looking values for *every one* of the $2^k$ possible items without storing any of them — a feat no PRG-based scheme achieves without scanning or storing an exponential table.

This combination — reproducibility without communication, unpredictability to outsiders — is why pseudorandom functions are the engine of secure **private-key encryption** and **message-authentication** schemes: a ciphertext or a tag is (or masks itself with) a value $f_s(\cdot)$ that the holder of the shared seed can recompute, and that anyone else cannot predict. It is also why PRFs power *negative* results in computational learning theory and circuit complexity (cf. Natural Proofs): their existence shows that no efficient test can certify "random-looking" behavior of the kind those theories would need.

## Why this matters

- **From strings to functions is a leap in access, not in assumptions.** Module 4 built generators from one-way functions; the next lesson (Theorem 2.18, GGM) shows that every PRG yields a PRF, so pseudorandom functions rest on exactly the same computational assumptions. What the seed buys grows from one long string to an exponential, directly accessible table.
- **The two directions have opposite difficulty.** This lesson's theorem (PRF $\Rightarrow$ PRG, sample at fixed points) is almost free — a one-line reduction. The converse (PRG $\Rightarrow$ PRF) is Theorem 2.18 and is genuinely hard: the GGM tree must fool *adaptive* oracle machines. Noticing this asymmetry tells you where the real work of the module lies.
- **The oracle model is this module's real definitional work.** Learning to reason about machines that may only query — and may query adaptively — is the skill the GGM hybrid proof will demand, and it generalizes: space-bounded and non-uniform distinguishers (Modules 6 and 7) are again just restricted classes of observers.
- **PRFs are the sharpest instance of the behavioristic view of randomness.** Revisit the reflections of §2.8: in the computational approach, randomness is defined by its *observer*. A PRF is an object that is ontologically a tiny deterministic machine — a seed plus an algorithm — yet behavioristically indistinguishable from a uniformly random function by any efficient interrogator. The Kolmogorov-style "true explanation" of the values of $f_s$ is simply $(s, \text{algorithm})$; the behavioristic verdict is "random". Distributions that are ontologically very different (deterministic seeds vs. uniform functions) are declared equivalent by the computational point of view.
- **Payoff ahead.** Encryption, message authentication, and challenge–response protocols all reduce to "evaluate the shared function"; learning theory and the Natural Proofs barrier reduce to "no efficient observer can tell $f_s$ from random". Both families of results are corollaries of a single definition — the one you can now state in full.

defs.name: Definition 2.17 (pseudorandom functions)
defs.statement:
A **pseudorandom function (ensemble)** is a collection of functions

$$\{\, f_s: \{0,1\}^{|s|} \to \{0,1\}^{|s|} \,\}_{s \in \{0,1\}^*}$$

that satisfies the following two conditions:

1. **(efficient evaluation)** There exists an efficient (deterministic) algorithm that, given a seed $s$ and an argument $x \in \{0,1\}^{|s|}$, returns $f_s(x)$.

2. **(pseudorandomness)** For every probabilistic polynomial-time oracle machine $M$, every positive polynomial $p(\cdot)$, and all sufficiently large $k$'s:

$$\left|\, \Pr\left[M^{f_{U_k}}\left(1^k\right) = 1\right] - \Pr\left[M^{F_k}\left(1^k\right) = 1\right] \,\right| < \frac{1}{p(k)}$$

where $U_k$ is uniformly distributed over $\{0,1\}^k$, the oracle $f_{U_k}$ is the function $f_s$ with the seed $s$ drawn uniformly from $\{0,1\}^k$, and $F_k$ denotes a uniformly selected function mapping $\{0,1\}^k$ to $\{0,1\}^k$. (Both probabilities are taken over the choice of oracle and over $M$'s internal coin tosses.)
defs.intuition: One $k$-bit seed names one function among $2^{k \cdot 2^k}$ possible functions — but only $2^k$ of them are 'in the family'. The pseudorandomness condition says no efficient oracle machine can tell oracle access to $f_s$ (random seed) from oracle access to a truly random function; efficient evaluation makes the object usable, and oracle access makes the definition meaningful, since a full description is exponentially long.

defs.name: The oracle indistinguishability game (function version)
defs.statement:
The testing procedure in Definition 2.17 is a **probabilistic polynomial-time oracle machine** $M$ run on input $1^k$. It interacts with an oracle as follows:

- $M$ is *not* given the seed $s$ and is *not* given any explicit description of the function under test — it has only black-box (oracle) access.
- In each round $M$ writes a query $x \in \{0,1\}^k$ and receives the answer $f(x) \in \{0,1\}^k$. Queries may be chosen **adaptively**: each query may depend on all previous answers and on $M$'s internal coin tosses.
- $M$ runs in time polynomial in $k$ and may ask any polynomial number $q = \mathrm{poly}(k)$ of queries; at the end it outputs a single verdict bit.

The two experiments are: (i) the oracle is $f_s$ for a uniformly random seed $s \leftarrow U_k$; (ii) the oracle is $F_k$, a uniformly random function from $\{0,1\}^k$ to $\{0,1\}^k$. The family is pseudorandom if no such $M$ makes the acceptance probabilities of the two experiments differ by a non-negligible amount.
defs.intuition: The oracle formulation is forced by the object: a function on $k$-bit strings has a $k \cdot 2^k$-bit description, and in the random-function experiment there is no seed to hand out, so a description (or the seed) can never be part of the distinguisher's input. Oracle access also mirrors applications, where parties share only the seed and interact with $f_s$ exclusively through queries. Because $M$ is probabilistic, the probabilities range over the oracle choice *and* over $M$'s coins; because the output is a single bit, nothing is lost by forbidding richer verdicts — a distinguisher is by definition a yes/no decision.

theorems.name: Folklore observation: pseudorandom functions yield pseudorandom generators
theorems.statement:
Let $\{f_s: \{0,1\}^{|s|} \to \{0,1\}^{|s|}\}_{s \in \{0,1\}^*}$ be a pseudorandom function ensemble. Let $m: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be polynomial-time computable with $2 \le m(k) \le 2^k$, and let $x_1, \ldots, x_{m(k)}$ be pairwise distinct elements of $\{0,1\}^k$ (e.g., the $k$-bit binary encodings of $1, \ldots, m(k)$). Define

$$G(s) \;=\; f_s(x_1) \, \circ \, f_s(x_2) \, \circ \, \cdots \, \circ \, f_s(x_{m(k)}),$$

the concatenation of the values of $f_s$ at those $m(k)$ fixed points. Then $G: \{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^{m(k) \cdot k}$ is a pseudorandom generator, with stretch $\ell(k) = m(k) \cdot k \ge 2k$.
theorems.intuition: One seed names many coherent 'virtual' pseudorandom strings at once: the table of $f_s$ at any fixed set of points is itself a pseudorandom string. This is the easy direction of PRF $\Leftrightarrow$ PRG; the hard converse (every PRG yields a PRF) is Theorem 2.18, the GGM construction, in the next lesson.
theorems.proof:
Let $D$ be any PPT distinguisher for $G$, and write its gap as

$$\varepsilon(k) = \left|\Pr[D(G(U_k)) = 1] - \Pr[D(U_{m(k) \cdot k}) = 1]\right|.$$

Build a probabilistic polynomial-time oracle machine $M$: on input $1^k$, query the oracle at $x_1, \ldots, x_{m(k)}$, concatenate the answers into a string $z$ of length $m(k) \cdot k$, and output $D(z)$ (running $D$ on $z$, using fresh internal coins). Two observations identify $M$'s gap with $D$'s:

1. If the oracle is $f_{U_k}$, then $z = f_{U_k}(x_1) \cdots f_{U_k}(x_{m(k)})$, which is distributed exactly as $G(U_k)$. Hence $\Pr[M^{f_{U_k}}(1^k) = 1] = \Pr[D(G(U_k)) = 1]$.

2. If the oracle is a uniformly random function $F_k$, then because $x_1, \ldots, x_{m(k)}$ are pairwise distinct, the answers $F_k(x_1), \ldots, F_k(x_{m(k)})$ are statistically independent, each uniform over $\{0,1\}^k$; their concatenation is therefore distributed exactly as $U_{m(k) \cdot k}$. Hence $\Pr[M^{F_k}(1^k) = 1] = \Pr[D(U_{m(k) \cdot k}) = 1]$.

Consequently $|\Pr[M^{f_{U_k}}(1^k) = 1] - \Pr[M^{F_k}(1^k) = 1]| = \varepsilon(k)$. Since $M$ is a PPT oracle machine making $m(k) = \mathrm{poly}(k)$ queries, the pseudorandomness condition of Definition 2.17 forces $\varepsilon(k) < 1/p(k)$ for every positive polynomial $p$ and all sufficiently large $k$ — i.e., $\varepsilon$ is negligible. As $D$ was arbitrary, $G$ is a pseudorandom generator. ∎

Two remarks. First, the queries $x_i$ are fixed in advance and $M$ never adapts them; this is legitimate because the definition quantifies over *all* PPT oracle machines, including non-adaptive ones with hard-wired query lists — adaptivity being permitted only makes the guarantee stronger. Second, pairwise distinctness of the $x_i$'s is used exactly in observation 2: a truly random function answers distinct points independently, whereas re-querying the same point would return the same value, ruining uniformity of the ideal string.

checkpoints.question: In Definition 2.17 the distinguisher M is given oracle access to a function rather than a description of it (or the seed). Which is the best explanation of why the definition is set up this way?

options.text: A function from {0,1}^k to {0,1}^k has a truth table of k·2^k bits, so an explicit description is exponentially long; moreover the seed s exists only in the pseudorandom experiment, so handing s to M would break the symmetry with the random-function experiment, where no seed exists. Oracle access is also exactly how PRFs are used: parties share only the seed and interact with f_s through queries.
Oracle machines are computationally weaker than ordinary machines, and weakening the distinguisher is the only way to make the definition satisfiable.
The seed is revealed to M through the oracle answers, so M always knows which function it is talking to and can verify efficiency directly.
Oracle access is a stylistic convention with no security content; giving M the full seed would define an equivalent, only slightly weaker notion.

checkpoints.explanation: The truth table of any function {0,1}^k -> {0,1}^k has k·2^k bits — exponential — so 'reading the description' is not a feasible way to test such an object, in the pseudorandom case or the random case alike. Giving the distinguisher the seed in the pseudorandom case would be worse than infeasible: it would be conceptually broken, because the random-function experiment has no seed to offer, destroying the symmetry between the two experiments the definition compares. (A distinguisher that knew s could evaluate f_s itself and would trivially separate the cases.) Oracle access is therefore the only faithful formalization of 'testing a function you never see', and it matches the applications, where a PRF is used purely through evaluations of the shared function.

checkpoints.question: Which statement correctly describes the query model in Definition 2.17?

options.text: M is a probabilistic polynomial-time machine that may choose its queries adaptively (each query may depend on earlier answers and on its own coins) and finally outputs a single verdict bit; restricting the output to one bit loses nothing, because a distinguisher is by definition a yes/no decision, and any richer test can be run internally and summarized in that bit.
M must fix all of its queries in advance, because adaptive queries would let M break any deterministic function such as f_s.
M must output one bit for each query it makes, so that its transcript can be compared answer-by-answer with the oracle's responses.
M is allowed at most a constant number of queries; anything more would make the gap bound 1/p(k) impossible to satisfy.

checkpoints.explanation: The definition deliberately allows adaptivity — each query may depend on previous answers — because adaptive strategies are strictly more powerful than fixed query lists (e.g., querying x and then f(x) detects relations no pre-planned list could target), and security against the stronger adversary is what applications need. One output bit is without loss of generality: a distinguisher is a binary decision; a machine with a richer output is converted by running it internally and emitting 1 exactly when its verdict is accepted. Nothing in the definition limits the number of queries to a constant — only to a polynomial, since M must run in polynomial time. Determinism of f_s does not neutralize adaptivity: consistent re-answers do not help, but the ability to aim later queries at points correlated with earlier answers does.

checkpoints.question: Two parties share the seed s of a pseudorandom function and later — with no communication at all — each must be able to produce 'the' random-looking value attached to an item v that arises on-line. Why does setting r_v = f_s(v) achieve this?

options.text: Because f_s is deterministic, both parties always compute the identical value f_s(v) from the shared seed, so agreement costs nothing; and by pseudorandomness, to any efficient party that does not know s — even one that chooses items adaptively after seeing earlier values — the function's values at distinct, unqueried points look like those of a truly random function, so each new v gets a value that looks freshly random while remaining consistent.
Because f_s(v) is freshly sampled from the uniform distribution over {0,1}^k each time any party evaluates it.
Because the parties first run a PRG until they have generated and stored the entire table of 2^k values of f_s, and then each looks up v in the stored table.
Because v is used as a one-time pad key to encrypt the seed, and the ciphertext is the agreed random value.

checkpoints.explanation: The scheme works precisely because f_s is a function (deterministic: same v always gives same value, so both parties agree without any message) that is pseudorandom (values at unqueried points look random even to an adaptive adversary). The two properties are exactly the two conditions of Definition 2.17: efficient evaluation makes computing r_v on demand possible, and oracle pseudorandomness guarantees that the association v -> r_v is indistinguishable from a truly random association. The wrong options violate the setup: f_s(v) is not freshly sampled (it is fixed by s — which is precisely what enables agreement), no exponential table is ever generated or stored (that would defeat the purpose of direct access), and encryption plays no role in defining the value.

exercises.prompt: Write out Definition 2.17 completely, making every quantifier explicit (do not let words like 'efficient' or 'negligible' carry the meaning), and then annotate each ingredient: (i) the ensemble {f_s} indexed by seeds; (ii) the efficient-evaluation condition; (iii) the oracle machine M, its input 1^k, and its internal coins; (iv) the reference object F_k; (v) the quantifier order 'for every PPT M, every positive polynomial p, all sufficiently large k'. For each ingredient, state what would go wrong — or become meaningless — if it were omitted or changed.
exercises.hint: A fully explicit rendering of condition (2) is: for every PPT oracle machine M, for every positive polynomial p(.), there exists k_0 such that for all k >= k_0, |Pr_{s<-U_k, coins}[M^{f_s}(1^k)=1] - Pr_{F, coins}[M^{F}(1^k)=1]| < 1/p(k), where F ranges over all functions {0,1}^k -> {0,1}^k uniformly. Test your reading by negating the definition: the family fails to be a PRF iff there exists a PPT M and a polynomial p such that the gap is at least 1/p(k) for infinitely many k. Use this 'negation discipline' to check each quantifier's position.

exercises.prompt: Show that pseudorandom functions yield pseudorandom generators. Let {f_s} be a PRF with f_s: {0,1}^k -> {0,1}^k, fix m(k) = 2k pairwise distinct inputs x_1, ..., x_{m(k)} in {0,1}^k (say the k-bit encodings of 1, ..., 2k), and define G(s) = f_s(x_1) f_s(x_2) ... f_s(x_{m(k)}) (concatenation). (i) State the stretch and why G is efficiently computable. (ii) Prove G is indistinguishable from uniform by a reduction to Definition 2.17. (iii) Explain explicitly why it is legitimate that the queries are fixed in advance rather than adaptive, and where the pairwise distinctness of the x_i's is used.
exercises.hint: Two observations do all the work. (a) For a truly random F_k, the values F_k(x_1), ..., F_k(x_m) at pairwise distinct points are independent and uniform over {0,1}^k, so their concatenation is distributed exactly as U_{m·k}. (b) An oracle machine that queries exactly x_1, ..., x_m and then feeds the concatenated answers to the alleged distinguisher D is a perfectly legal machine in Definition 2.17 — the definition quantifies over all PPT oracle machines, adaptive or not. Stretch: output length is m(k)·k = 2k^2 > k; more generally any poly-bounded m(k) >= 2 works.

exercises.prompt: Analyze the query model of Definition 2.17. (a) Define precisely what an adaptive oracle machine is and contrast it with a non-adaptive one; give a concrete test that can only be phrased adaptively. (b) Argue why the one-bit output of the definition is without loss of generality — why allowing M to output, say, a long string or a real-valued statistic adds no distinguishing power. (c) Since the function being queried is deterministic, why does adaptivity still add power? Illustrate with a pair of function families that an adaptive machine can separate with two queries but no non-adaptive machine can separate with polynomially many.
exercises.hint: (a) Non-adaptive: the whole list (q_1, ..., q_t) is chosen before any answer is seen. Adaptive: q_{i+1} is chosen as a function of (q_1, a_1, ..., q_i, a_i) and coins. (b) Acceptance is a predicate of the full transcript; let the one-bit machine run the multi-output machine internally and output 1 iff the verdict is accepted. (c) Determinism only means repeated queries give consistent answers — consistency is automatic and cannot separate anything. Adaptivity lets the machine aim at correlated points. Example: compare a random involution (f(f(x)) = x for all x) with a truly random function: two queries x, then f(x), check f(f(x)) = x — always true for an involution, true with probability only 2^{-k} for a random function. A non-adaptive machine sees only q distinct random-looking answers in both cases and cannot tell them apart with poly(k) queries.
